## Observation

For any forest \(G\) with at least one edge, \(\operatorname{tw}(G[K_2])=3\).

## Proof

For each edge \(uv\) of \(G\), use a bag containing both copies of \(u\) and both copies of \(v\). Connect the bags for edges incident to each vertex in a tree. Since \(G\) is a forest, these connections form a forest; connect its components arbitrarily. Every edge of \(G[K_2]\) lies in a bag, and the bags containing either copy of a vertex form a connected subtree. This gives treewidth at most \(3\). Any edge of \(G\) yields a \(K_4\) in \(G[K_2]\), so treewidth is at least \(3\).

This is a proved special case of the manuscript’s width identity, derived from the stated definitions. It is not recorded as a proof-state update, and the transcript does not establish that it closes a recorded obligation. No computation or independent review was performed.

## Observation

The assigned question is Q-08a1c5b68f. The binding specification requires fixing both state width \(S\) and decoder cost \(D\) when reporting an update-cost minimum. It also distinguishes full search semantics from the weaker live/dead separation variant.

## Established

For full search semantics, at any layer \(t\), if there are \(L_t\) live prefixes and at least one dead prefix, then a correct machine needs at least \(L_t+1\) distinct states: each live prefix must have its own state, and dead prefixes must not share one of those states. With \(S_t\) state bits there are at most \(2^{S_t}\) states, so
\[
S_t \ge \left\lceil \log_2(L_t+1)\right\rceil.
\]
If there are no dead prefixes, the same counting argument gives \(S_t\ge\lceil\log_2 L_t\rceil\). This is a state-counting bound, not an update-gate lower bound.

**Observation:** For deterministic search from a final state \(q:X\to Q\), suppose \(Z\subseteq X\) consists of YES inputs such that no single witness is valid for two distinct inputs in \(Z\). Then \(q\) is injective on \(Z\).

**Proof:** If distinct \(x,y\in Z\) had \(q(x)=q(y)\), the deterministic decoder would return the same witness on both inputs. That witness would be valid for both, contradicting the defining property of \(Z\). Hence \(|Q|\ge |Z|\). For an \(S\)-bit state, \(S\ge\lceil\log_2|Z|\rceil\).

For Search-MCSP, each circuit computes one truth table, so the full YES set is witness-separated; this recovers \(S\ge\lceil\log_2|Y|\rceil\), including for affine state maps. This is a restricted search-state lemma, not a lower bound for general streaming algorithms or progress toward \(P\ne NP\).

## Observation

For a fixed suffix \(z\), let \(W(p,z)\) be the set of valid witnesses for input \(pz\). Suppose a deterministic streaming machine’s final decoder depends only on its final state and is correct whenever \(W(p,z)\neq\varnothing\).

## Lemma

If equal-length prefixes \(p_1,\ldots,p_k\) have nonempty, pairwise disjoint sets \(W(p_i,z)\), then they reach distinct states after reading their prefixes. Hence the machine has at least \(k\) states.

**Proof.** If two prefixes reached the same state, processing the common suffix \(z\) would lead to the same final state and decoded output. That output would have to belong to both prefixes’ disjoint witness sets, a contradiction. ∎

## Scope and continuation

This proves a state-capacity bound for a final-state-only decoder. It does not bound transition gate cost, establish that such a prefix family exists for \(SC_{n,s}\), or imply \(P\ne NP\).
